intro: This last unit brings the course together. You will read two famous passages in full. In Kiddushin 30b-32a, the rabbis ask what it means to honor and revere parents, and they learn from a jeweler in Ashkelon. In Eruvin 13b, two schools argue for three years, and a heavenly voice calls both sides the words of the living God.

Then you will do what the Talmud does. With a partner, in chavruta, you will choose a sugya, map its moves, bring in Rashi, Tosafot and a modern reader, and present both sides. Your thesis will name what the argument decides and whom the ruling protects.

By the end, you will be able to read a whole sugya, cite it by tractate and page, attribute every view to its reader and argue fairly with someone who disagrees. Those are the course's two threads, argument and mercy, in your own hands.
bigQuestion: How can a text that keeps its arguments open still guide people toward what is right and kind?

timeline.t: Hillel and Shammai teach in Jerusalem; their schools will argue for generations
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Tarfon teach, as the rabbis regroup after the Temple's fall in 70 CE
The Mishnah is edited under Rabbi Judah the Prince
Rashi writes his commentary in Troyes, France
The Tosafists of France and Germany add their comments
The Vilna edition sets the standard printed Talmud page
Abington v. Schempp allows objective study of religion in public schools
Tens of thousands mark a Siyum HaShas at MetLife Stadium

words.d: one unit of Talmudic discussion, moving through question, proof, objection and answer
study in pairs; from the Aramaic word for companion
kibbud; active care for a parent, such as food, clothing and help getting around
mora; respect shown by restraint, such as not taking a parent's seat
a heavenly voice in rabbinic stories
the school of Hillel, whose rulings usually became Jewish law
a teaching of the Mishnah's era not included in the Mishnah
the anonymous voice of the Gemara
medieval 'additions' by scholars in France and Germany, printed on the outer margin
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040-1105), the most widely read Talmud commentator
the main claim a presentation argues for
a view the law does not follow, which the Talmud still records

test.q: Which tractate contains the story of Dama ben Netina?
What is the difference between honor and reverence in Kiddushin 31b?
choices: Honor is for mothers; reverence is for fathers
Honor is aggadah; reverence is halakhah
Honor is active care; reverence is restraint
test.why: The baraita lists feeding and clothing as honor and not taking a parent's seat as reverence.

test.q: Whose money pays for a parent's food, according to the ruling in Kiddushin 32a?
test.why: The Gemara rules for the parent's money; later codes add that a child with means helps a parent without.

test.q: Which verse do the rabbis use to limit a parent's commands?
test.why: Leviticus 19:3 joins reverence for parents with keeping God's Sabbaths.

test.q: How long did Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue, according to Eruvin 13b?
test.why: Eruvin 13b says the dispute lasted three years.

test.q: Why does the Gemara say the law follows Beit Hillel?
choices: They were the majority in Rome
They were humble and taught Beit Shammai's view first
test.why: Eruvin 13b credits their gentleness and humility.

test.q: Which passage has a rabbi answer a heavenly voice with 'It is not in heaven'?
test.why: In the oven of Akhnai story, Rabbi Yehoshua quotes Deuteronomy 30:12.

test.q: What does Mishnah Eduyot 1:5 say about minority views?
choices: They are kept so a later court may rely on them
test.why: Eduyot 1:5 preserves them for future courts.

choices: A tanna of the first century
test.why: Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, taught in Troyes.

test.q: Where do Tosafot appear on the printed page?
choices: At the top of the Mishnah
test.why: Tosafot run on the outer side; Rashi on the inner.
Chavruta is paired study, praised in Taanit 7a and 23a.

test.q: What should a capstone thesis name?
choices: What the argument decides and what the ruling protects
test.why: It follows the course's two threads, argument and mercy.

test.q: Which sentence fits the course's neutral stance?
choices: Both schools spoke words of the living God
Rabbinic tradition holds that both schools spoke words of the living God
We know Beit Hillel was right
test.why: The course attributes beliefs to their tradition without asserting or denying them.
Rodkinson is public domain, though abridged and uneven.

test.q: What does the anonymous 'stam' do in the Gemara?
choices: Asks and answers without naming a rabbi
test.why: The stam is the Gemara's unnamed voice.

write.prompt: Does the Talmud value agreement or disagreement more? Cite two or three passages from this unit, such as Kiddushin 31a-32a, Eruvin 13b and Mishnah Eduyot 1:5. Explain what each says and how different readers have understood it.
tips: Name each text by tractate and page, and name the translation you read.
Attribute every belief: 'the Gemara says', 'Rashi explains', 'historians argue'.
Give the minority view a fair hearing, as the Talmud does.
Compare readings rather than judging which tradition is right.
Use the unit's terms: sugya, baraita, bat kol, chavruta.
